prompt: Asked what E-4104 means, which section did sections.py rank first?

choices.text: affiliate-api > Endpoints
choices.why: Not in the top three at all.

choices.text: affiliate-api > Changes in 2.3
choices.why: Right, at 0.478: it talks about an error and a version, like the question.

choices.text: affiliate-api > Errors
choices.why: The error table came second, at 0.393.

choices.text: affiliate-api > Rate limits
choices.why: Third, at 0.380.

prompt: The model answered the E-4104 question correctly, from the table ranked second. What does the lesson say that hides?
hint: Which half nearly failed?

choices.text: The search ranked the change log above the table, because codes one character apart look alike to it
choices.why: Right. The model read the exact string once it was there; a corpus with more near-misses would have left the table out.

choices.text: The question was too short to embed
choices.why: Any text can be embedded; the issue is what the vector captures.

choices.text: The error table did not contain E-4104
choices.why: It did: grep found it on line 85.

choices.text: The model guessed the meaning from its training
choices.why: Its answer is the table's row, word for word; it read it from the prompt.

prompt: The rate-limit section came second, and its sentence "A key may make 120 requests per minute" never says rate or limit. What put it in the top three?
hint: Which part of the section uses the question's words?

choices.text: Its heading, which the section was embedded with
choices.why: Right. Cut away from its heading, the text no longer says what it is about; lesson 5 keeps the heading with every chunk.

choices.text: The search used a larger k for this kind of question
choices.why: k was 3, as for every question in the lesson.

choices.text: The number 120 matched the question
choices.why: The question has no number in it.

choices.text: The model asked for it
choices.why: The search runs before the model sees anything.

prompt: Exact strings such as error codes and flags are what ___ search was built to find.
hint: The kind of search grep does.

prompt: A developer on version 2.2 of the affiliate API asks how to filter search results by language. What should a well-built assistant do?
hint: 2.2 ignores lang.

choices.text: Answer with the error E-4105, which version 2.3 added
choices.why: E-4105 is about campaign labels, not languages.

choices.text: Refuse, because questions about versions are out of scope
choices.why: The documents answer it; refusing throws away a correct answer.

choices.text: Explain the lang parameter, since it is in the reference
choices.why: That answer is right for 2.3 and wrong for this reader.

choices.text: Say lang exists from 2.3, and that 2.2 ignores it
choices.why: Right. The version belongs beside the chunk so the answer can say which version it is about.

prompt: What made the help centre articles easy material for retrieval?
hint: Compare them with the policies.

choices.text: Each answers one question in the customer's words
choices.why: Right, under a title that says what it answers.

choices.text: They are longer than the policy documents
choices.why: They are much shorter: about forty words each.

choices.text: They have no dates, so they never go out of date
choices.why: Every article has an updated date, and prices in them change.

choices.text: They are stored as JSON lines rather than as Markdown files
choices.why: The file format does not change how they embed.

prompt: For "como devolvo um livro", the Portuguese article on returns came first. What came second and third?
hint: Look at the language column.

choices.text: The other two Portuguese articles, about passwords and delivery
choices.why: Right: Portuguese matched Portuguese by spelling, whatever the subject.

choices.text: Two English articles about returns
choices.why: No English article reached the top three for either Portuguese question.

choices.text: The English versions of that same article, ranked just below it in order
choices.why: An English-only model cannot carry the question across languages.

choices.text: Nothing, because the search found no match
choices.why: A search always returns its top k.

prompt: Marginalia starts receiving questions in Spanish and has no Spanish documents. With all-MiniLM-L6-v2 as the embedding model, what should the team expect?
hint: What did the Portuguese questions reach?

choices.text: Near the Portuguese articles, by spelling
choices.why: Right: the model matches by word pieces, and Spanish shares many with Portuguese.

choices.text: The model will translate them before embedding
choices.why: An embedding model translates nothing.

choices.text: Spanish questions will reach the English articles, since Spanish is close to Portuguese
choices.why: Closeness to Portuguese does not help them reach English text.

choices.text: The search will refuse them as an unknown language
choices.why: A search never refuses; it returns its nearest k.

prompt: Why does the lesson count a refusal as better than a guess in customer support?
hint: What does a customer do with an answer?

choices.text: Refusals are cheaper to generate
choices.why: The cost of the reply's tokens is not the argument.

choices.text: A wrong answer becomes a promise the shop is then held to
choices.why: Right, and a screenshot of it can travel.

choices.text: The law forbids automated answers to customers
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: Customers prefer to talk to a person
choices.why: Maybe, but the argument is what a wrong answer commits the shop to.

prompt: For "When is the contract of sale formed?", which section scored highest?
hint: It was a contract, but not the terms of sale.

choices.text: terms-of-sale > 11. Changes to these terms
choices.why: It was not in the top three.

choices.text: terms-of-sale > 2. Placing an order
choices.why: That one came second, at 0.407, and held the answer.

choices.text: seller-agreement > 9. Ending the agreement
choices.why: Right, at 0.458: every contract sounds like every other.

choices.text: affiliate-api > Commission
choices.why: Third, at 0.402.

prompt: Clause 2.2 says the contract is formed when "we" send the email. The reply said "the seller" sends it. What does that show?
hint: Who is "we" in Marginalia's terms?

choices.text: A paraphrase can change the one word that binds
choices.why: Right. Marginalia is "we"; on a marketplace the seller is somebody else. A legal answer quotes, and a check confirms the quote.

choices.text: The search returned the seller agreement first
choices.why: It did, but the reply answered from the terms of sale, [2].

choices.text: The clause number was lost
choices.why: The reply kept section 2.2; the wording is what changed.

choices.text: The model had no source for the answer
choices.why: It had clause 2.2 in front of it and reworded it.

prompt: A customer disputes an order placed in November 2025, and the index holds only version 9 of the terms, in force from January 2026. What is the right behaviour?
hint: Clause 11.1 says which terms apply.

choices.text: Paraphrase version 9 so it reads as general advice
choices.why: A paraphrase of the wrong version is wrong twice.

choices.text: Quote version 9, since it is the current one
choices.why: Clause 11.1: the terms in force on the day of the order apply, and version 9 was not.

choices.text: Combine version 9 with the 2025 returns policy
choices.why: A returns policy is not the terms of sale, and mixing documents invents a contract.

choices.text: Say the terms for that date are not in the documents
choices.why: Right. A legal system keeps every version with its dates and refuses when it lacks the one that applies.

prompt: Which of these does a legal retrieval system need? Choose all that apply.
hint: Location, wording, scope.

choices.text: Verbatim quotes checked against the source
choices.why: Yes: a paraphrase has no legal force.

choices.text: Answers in the model's own words, for readability
choices.why: Readable and not binding; lawyers need the text that binds.

choices.text: A filter by document set and date
choices.why: Yes: every contract sounds like every other.

choices.text: The version and the clause in every citation
choices.why: Yes: the citation is half of a legal answer.

choices.text: A model that rewrites clauses in plain language
choices.why: That produces a new text with no force, wrong in the word that mattered.

prompt: By the uniq -c count, how many of the thirteen documents are public?
hint: audience: public

prompt: The fraud-review question leaked the finance threshold. What did the lesson say went wrong in the pipeline?
hint: Search, generation, or something else?

choices.text: The generator invented the 0.82 threshold from what it learnt in training
choices.why: It quoted it faithfully from the finance document.

choices.text: The search ranked the sections in the wrong order
choices.why: It ranked the best section first; that is the problem.

choices.text: The question was phrased to trick the system
choices.why: It was an ordinary, reasonable question from a support desk.

choices.text: Nothing; one index with no idea who asks is the design flaw
choices.why: Right. Every step worked, and the boundary the document relied on was gone.

prompt: Why does the lesson reject a system prompt saying "do not reveal confidential information" as the fix?
hint: Where is the text by then?

choices.text: It would make the model refuse every question
choices.why: Not necessarily; the objection is that it does not hold, not that it overreaches.

choices.text: The finance document would stop being retrieved
choices.why: An instruction in the prompt changes nothing about the search.

choices.text: Providers do not allow that instruction in system prompts
choices.why: Any instruction is allowed; the problem is what it can guarantee.

choices.text: The text is already disclosed to the model, and an instruction does not hold
choices.why: Right, and nothing in the request says who the reader is.

prompt: Put in order what keeps a finance-only chunk away from a support agent.
hint: The decision is made before the search.
items: At indexing, copy each document's audience onto its chunks
At sign-in, know the user's role
At search time, keep only chunks that role may read
Build the prompt from what is left
trap: Filtering after the prompt is built is too late: the text has already been disclosed to the model.

hint: One kind of search is for exact strings.

pairs.right: vector, scoped to one document set
vector, filtered by who is asking

right_distractors: no search, the whole corpus every time

prompt: Which two uses fail by revealing rather than by being wrong?
hint: A correct answer to the wrong person.

choices.text: Legal and internal knowledge
choices.why: Right: an old version quoted as current, or a document shown to someone not cleared.

choices.text: Documentation and internal knowledge
choices.why: Documentation's failure is a wrong answer found quickly.

choices.text: Customer support and legal
choices.why: Support's worst case is a wrong promise, not a disclosure.

choices.text: Documentation and customer support
choices.why: Those fail mainly by being wrong.

prompt: A team plans to add the audience and version of each document to the index "once the assistant is popular". What does the lesson say about the timing?
hint: What does adding a field to every chunk require later?

choices.text: Later is fine, since metadata changes nothing about how retrieval ranks
choices.why: Metadata is what filters use; without it, the leak and the stale version stay.

choices.text: Only legal teams need it, so it can wait
choices.why: Internal knowledge needs audience just as much.

choices.text: Later means re-indexing all of it
choices.why: Right. Lesson 5 stores audience, owner, version and status from the start.

choices.text: Metadata belongs in the prompt, not the index
choices.why: A filter needs it in the index, before the prompt exists.

prompt: Why could the search not answer "Which documents mention a 14-day limit?" even with perfect ranking?
hint: How many documents does grep list, and how many results does the search return?

choices.text: The model refuses questions with a number in them
choices.why: It did not refuse; it answered, wrongly, from three sections.

choices.text: The phrase 14 days is not in any document
choices.why: grep found it in four.

choices.text: Numbers cannot be searched
choices.why: grep searched the number exactly.

choices.text: Four documents match and k = 3 returns three
choices.why: Right, and nothing in the output says the list was cut short.

prompt: A team copies each day's order statuses into a document so the assistant can retrieve them. What does the lesson predict?
hint: How often does an order status change?

choices.text: Better answers, since the statuses are now text
choices.why: They are text that is out of date by the next minute.

choices.text: Stale numbers delivered with citations
choices.why: Right: the status lives in the order system and changes by the minute; call it directly.

choices.text: A leak of other customers' orders to everyone
choices.why: A real risk too, but not the one the lesson names here.

choices.text: A refusal for every order question
choices.why: The search would find something; it would just be old.

prompt: Which signal does the lesson give for spotting a question retrieval cannot answer?
hint: Look at the scores in this lesson's last runs.

choices.text: A question in Portuguese
choices.why: Language is a coverage problem, not a sign the answer is unwritten.

choices.text: A question longer than ten words
choices.why: Length says nothing about where the answer lives.

choices.text: A low top score
choices.why: Right: under 0.42 for both, against 0.72 and 0.698 for answerable ones.

choices.text: A reply with more than one citation
choices.why: Several citations are normal for answerable questions.

prompt: Which use does the lesson suggest a team start with, and why?
hint: The one whose failures a person can fix and whose text is public.

choices.text: Support over the public help centre
choices.why: Right: short public articles and a measure of success in tickets answered.

choices.text: Internal knowledge, because nobody can find anything
choices.why: It is valuable and needs permissions before the first user.

choices.text: Documentation, because engineers check the answers
choices.why: It comes second, and needs lexical search early.

choices.text: Legal, because its documents are the most structured
choices.why: Structure helps, but legal needs version and permission machinery first.
